The indictment says Smith had been a musician with a catalog of his own, and it quotes prosecutors saying he carried out the scheme to generate millions of dollars in royalties from fraudulent streaming.

Smith agreed to forfeit $8,091,843.64, which the DOJ said represented the proceeds of the fraudulent streaming scheme, and the plea was announced by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.

Smith pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and faced a maximum sentence of five years in prison under the plea announced by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.

The scheme allegedly ran from approximately 2017 through 2024, the indictment was filed in September 2024, and the guilty plea was announced on March 19, 2026; the investigation appears to have originated from prosecutors’ review of royalty inflation across streaming platforms.

After the scheme was exposed, Smith faced a forfeiture obligation of more than $8 million and federal felony prosecution, with reporting describing him as out on bail while the case moved toward trial.

The indictment identifies Smith’s co-conspirators as a music publicist, the CEO of an unnamed AI music company, and a music promoter, all of whom were involved in creating and moving the AI-generated songs.

U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton said Smith’s guilty plea was for a scheme to defraud music streaming platforms and musicians of royalty payments, announced in the Southern District of New York plea release.
At the height of the scheme, Michael Smith used over a thousand bot accounts simultaneously to artificially boost streams, and those bots streamed his AI-generated songs billions of times.
Smith’s bot accounts were capable of generating approximately 661,440 streams per day.

The case was publicly triggered by the Southern District of New York and the FBI announcing the unsealing of a three-count indictment on September 4, 2024, charging Smith with wire fraud conspiracy, wire fraud, and money laundering conspiracy.

The indictment says Smith allegedly used artificial intelligence to create hundreds of thousands of songs and bots to stream them billions of times, exploiting royalty payments paid by streaming platforms for reported plays.
A comparable case cited in coverage is the 2026 Michael Smith prosecution itself, described as the first major criminal conviction for AI-assisted music streaming fraud in the United States.

The case record shows that from approximately 2017 through 2024 Michael Smith orchestrated the scheme, buying hundreds of thousands of AI-generated songs and using bots to stream them billions of times, while the indictment was unsealed on September 4, 2024 and he later pleaded guilty on March 19, 2026.

The record says Smith used financial accounts and payment systems to receive royalty payouts, then moved the proceeds through accounts in the names of shell companies, including Arranged Alliance LLC, in transactions totaling more than $10 million in royalties and over $8 million in forfeiture.
The scheme ran from approximately 2017 up to and including 2024.
The case is filed in the Southern District of New York, case number 24 Cr. 504.
The indictment contains three counts: Count One (Conspiracy to Commit Wire Fraud), Count Two (Wire Fraud), and Count Three (Money Laundering Conspiracy).
SMITH purchased from a coconspirator hundreds of thousands of songs created through artificial intelligence ('AI').
SMITH uploaded the AI-generated songs to Streaming Platforms including Amazon Music, Apple Music, Spotify, and YouTube Music.
SMITH used 'bots'—automated programs—to stream the AI-generated songs billions of times.
At the height of the scheme, SMITH used over a thousand bot accounts simultaneously.
SMITH fraudulently obtained more than $10 million in royalty payments.
Royalty payments per stream are often less than one cent per stream.
Federal regulations at 37 C.F.R. §§ 385.2 and 385.21 provide that manipulated streams are not eligible for royalties.

Streaming Platform-1's User Guidelines prohibited 'artificially increasing play counts or follow counts, artificially promoting Content, or other manipulation including by (i) using any bot, script, or other automated process.'
Distribution Company-1 is described as a Manhattan-based music distribution company.

Distribution Company-1 required customers to 'agree not to engage in (or to permit, encourage, enlist, retain, or employ third parties to engage in), activities that, in [Distribution Company-1]'s sole discretion, constitute Streaming Manipulation.'

Distribution Company-1 defined streaming manipulation as 'any activity and/or method which involves the artificial creation, by human or non-human means, of online or offline plays on audio and/or audio-visual streaming services, where such plays do not represent bona fide end-user listening and/or views initiated by genuine consumers and taking place in the reporting country.'
Distribution Company-2 is described as a Florida-based music distribution company.

Distribution Company-2 required customers to 'represent and warrant' they would not engage in 'so-called illegal boosting, fraudulent streaming, or juicing activities or any similar activities designed to artificially inflate the amount of streams.'
On or about March 3, 2023, SMITH falsely represented to Distribution Company-2 that he would not engage in fraudulent streaming.

The fraud proceeded in three stages: (1) creating Bot Accounts, (2) using software to cause Bot Accounts to continuously stream songs SMITH owned, and (3) collecting royalties based on fraudulent streams.
SMITH obtained thousands of email accounts ('Fake Email Accounts') purchased from vendors who sold bulk email accounts, often in the names of fictitious identities.
SMITH used the Fake Email Accounts to create and register Bot Accounts on the Streaming Platforms, typically in fake names corresponding to the Fake Email Accounts.
At certain points, SMITH had as many as 10,000 active Bot Accounts on the Streaming Platforms.
SMITH paid individuals located abroad as well as coconspirators located in the United States to do the data entry work of signing up for the Bot Accounts.

In a May 11, 2017 email to coconspirator CC-1, SMITH asked CC-1 to create Bot Accounts on a particular Streaming Platform: 'Make up names and addresses[.] [J]ust make sure they all are the same for family member and also make sure everyone is over 18.'
SMITH typically paid for 'family plans' on the Streaming Platforms to maximize streams, as family plans cost less per user than individual plans.
SMITH used a Manhattan-based service ('Financial Service-1') that provided large numbers of debit cards, typically corporate debit cards for employees of a company.
SMITH lied to Financial Service-1 and provided it with dozens of fake names corresponding to the Fake Email Accounts and Bot Accounts, claiming those fake names belonged to employees of his company.
SMITH used more than $1.3 million in fraudulently obtained royalties to fund the debit cards.

In multiple transactions from approximately 2020 through 2023, SMITH transferred $1.3 million in fraudulently obtained royalties to a bank account he controlled at a U.S.-based financial institution in the name of SMH Entertainment.
SMITH then transferred the proceeds from the SMH Entertainment account to Financial Service-1 to fund debit cards for the Bot Accounts.
SMITH used cloud computer services to use many virtual computers at the same time.
SMITH used some of the Bot Accounts on each virtual computer simultaneously, using web players for each Streaming Platform with multiple Bot Accounts streaming on separate browser tabs.
SMITH purchased and subsequently modified 'macros'—small pieces of computer code that automatically continuously played the music.
On October 20, 2017, SMITH emailed himself a financial breakdown of his streaming operation.
In the October 20, 2017 self-email, SMITH wrote he had 52 cloud services accounts, each with 20 Bot Accounts, for a total of 1,040 Bot Accounts.
In the October 20, 2017 self-email, SMITH wrote each Bot Account could stream approximately 636 songs per day, for a total of approximately 661,440 streams per day.
SMITH estimated the average royalty per stream was half of one cent ($0.005), yielding daily royalties of $3,307.20, monthly royalties of $99,216, and annual royalties of $1,207,128.
SMITH caused the Bot Accounts to log in using different virtual private networks ('VPNs') to conceal that the Bot Accounts were all operating from SMITH's home.
SMITH directed his coconspirators that the Bot Accounts and macros be 'Unde[te]ctable: At least put every safety measure in to avoid detection.'
SMITH spread his automated streams across thousands of songs to avoid anomalous streaming as to any single song.
On or about October 4, 2018, SMITH emailed two coconspirators: 'in order to not raise any issues with the powers that be we need a TON of content with small amounts of Streams.'

On or about May 9, 2019, SMITH emailed a coconspirator: 'I can't run the bots without content. And I need enough content so I don't overrun each song. That's the problem. If we get too many streams on one song it comes down.'
Early in the scheme, SMITH used the catalog of a music publicist designated as CC-2 to fraudulently generate royalty payments.
SMITH later attempted to sell his fraudulent streaming scheme as a service, in which other musicians would pay him for streams or share royalties in exchange for fraudulent streams of their music.
In or about 2018, SMITH began working with the Chief Executive Officer of an AI music company designated as CC-3 and a music promoter designated as CC-4.
SMITH began manipulating streams of AI-generated music in or about October 2018.
CC-4 described the initial streams of the AI music as 'proof of concept.'
As of October 18, 2018, SMITH reported he had generated hundreds of thousands of streams of the AI music, and CC-4 replied, 'we've proved the model works.'
CC-3 began providing SMITH with thousands of songs each week to upload to the Streaming Platforms.
In a March 11, 2019 email to SMITH, CC-3 wrote: 'Keep in mind what we're doing musically here... this is not music, it's instant music ;).'
By June 5, 2019, SMITH reported to CC-3 and CC-4: 'We are at 88 million TOTAL STREAMS so far!!!'
As of June 5, 2019, SMITH's fraudulent streams were earning approximately $110,000 per month.
CC-3 and CC-4 were each receiving 10% of the fraud proceeds as of June 5, 2019.
On June 5, 2019, SMITH asked CC-3 to provide another 10,000 AI songs so he could 'spread this out more' to evade detection.
On or about February 1, 2019, SMITH and CC-3 entered into a 'Master Services Agreement.'
Under the Master Services Agreement, CC-3's AI music company agreed to provide SMITH with between 1,000 to 10,000 songs each month.
Under the Master Services Agreement, SMITH would have full ownership of the intellectual property rights in the songs.

Under the Master Services Agreement, SMITH agreed to provide metadata including song and artist names, and to pay CC-3's company each month the greater of $2,000 or 15% of the streaming revenue generated from the AI songs.
CC-3's songs were typically given file names that were a randomized list of letters and numbers, such as 'n_7a2b2d74-1621-4385-895d-b1e4af78d860.mp3.'

An alphabetically consecutive selection of 25 AI song names SMITH used includes: 'Zygophyceae,' 'Zygophyllaceae,' 'Zygophyllum,' 'Zygopteraceae,' 'Zygopteris,' 'Zygopteron,' 'Zygopterous,' 'Zygosporic,' 'Zygotenes,' 'Zygotes,' 'Zygotic,' 'Zygotic Lanie,' 'Zygotic Washstands,' 'Zyme Bedewing,' 'Zymes,' 'Zymite,' 'Zymo Phyte,' 'Zymogenes,' 'Zymogenic,' 'Zymologies,' 'Zymoplastic,' 'Zymopure,' 'Zymotechnical,' 'Zymotechny,' and 'Zyzomys.'

An alphabetically consecutive selection of 25 AI artist names SMITH used includes: 'Calliope Bloom,' 'Calliope Erratum,' 'Callous,' 'Callous Humane,' 'Callous Post,' 'Callousness,' 'Calm Baseball,' 'Calm Connected,' 'Calm Force,' 'Calm Identity,' 'Calm Innovation,' 'Calm Knuckles,' 'Calm Market,' 'Calm The Super,' 'Calm Weary,' 'Calms Scorching,' 'Calorie Event,' 'Calorie Screams,' 'Calvin Mann,' 'Calvinistic Dust,' 'Calypso Xored,' 'Camalus Disen,' 'Camaxtli Minerva,' 'Cambists Cagelings,' and 'Camel Edible.'

In an August 17, 2020 email, CC-3 wrote to SMITH: 'Song quality is 10x-20x better now, and we also have vocal generation capabilities. . . . Have a listen to the attached for an idea of what I'm talking about.'
In a February 2024 email, SMITH boasted that his 'existing music has generated at this point over 4 billion streams and $12 million in royalties since 2019.'
On or about March 6, 2018, Distribution Company-1 informed SMITH that one of his songs 'fit the criteria that is usually linked to store end streaming abuse.'
SMITH responded to Distribution Company-1 on March 6, 2018: 'I acknowledge what you wrote and I ask that you still release it. We have no intentions of committing streaming fraud.'
In or about October 2018, Distribution Company-1 advised SMITH it had received 'multiple reports of streaming abuse from different stores' and planned to remove SMITH's releases from all stores.
In response to Distribution Company-1's October 2018 warning, SMITH claimed: 'This is absolutely wrong and crazy! . . . There is absolutely no fraud going on whatsoever! How can I appeal this?'
In or about March 2019, Streaming Platform-1 informed Distribution Company-3 that it believed SMITH had engaged in streaming fraud.
Distribution Company-3 is identified as a music distribution company SMITH was working with at the time of the March 2019 notification.

When told of Streaming Platform-1's determination, SMITH falsely told Distribution Company-3: 'I have done NOTHING to artificially inflate the streams on my two albums. . . . I have not a done a thing to illegally stream my music. . . . I have not violated the terms of my agreement with you at all and you have provided no proof either. I have not illegally streamed my music.'

SMITH communicated directly with Streaming Platform-1 to deny streaming fraud and demand reinstatement of his music, writing: 'I need to see some proof as to why you are claiming I had artificial Streams? You have slandered me to my distributors claiming I've had fraudulent streams, however you have provided no proof to this claim, you have provided me no chance to defend myself, and you have withheld money that is owed to me. I am asking for you to provide me with the documentation of what you feel was done artificially. I have never done anything to artificially inflate my streams. I have worked with promotion companies who claim to be legitimate.'
The indictment charges Count One under Title 18, United States Code, Section 1349 (conspiracy to commit wire fraud).
